title: Fgf10 germline null - the canonical tetra-amelia mouse
mechanism: FGF10 is the mesenchymal signal that induces and sustains the apical ectodermal ridge (AER); it acts epistatically upstream of Fgf8, the earliest AER marker. Without it the AER never forms, the ZPA never forms, and the limb bud makes no outgrowth. The same ligand drives branching morphogenesis in lung, so the mouse has no lungs either.
intervention: Germline Fgf10 knockout (two independent lines published, 1998 and 1999).
predicted_phenotype: AMELIA. Fetuses develop to birth with complete absence of both fore- and hindlimbs. The clavicle is unaffected (it is a dermal bone of different origin). Perinatal lethal from complete absence of lungs: the trachea forms, main-stem bronchial formation and all subsequent branching do not.

evidence.cite: Min H et al. 1998, Genes Dev 12:3156-61, 'Fgf-10 is required for both limb and lung development...'
evidence.finding: 'Limb bud initiation was abolished in Fgf-10(-/-) mice. Strikingly, Fgf-10(-/-) fetuses continued to develop until birth, despite the complete absence of both fore- and hindlimbs. Fgf-10 is necessary for apical ectodermal ridge (AER) formation and acts epistatically upstream of Fgf-8.' Perinatal lethality with complete absence of lungs.

evidence.cite: Sekine K et al. 1999, Nat Genet 21:138-41, 'Fgf10 is essential for limb and lung formation'
evidence.finding: 'complete truncation of the fore- and hindlimbs. In Fgf10-/- embryos, limb bud formation was initiated but outgrowth of the limb buds did not occur ... the apical ectodermal ridge (AER) and the zone of polarizing activity (ZPA) did not form'; clavicle formation unaffected; died at birth from lack of lung development.

reversibility: None. Germline, constitutive, and the animal cannot be rescued because the lung defect is independent of the limb defect.
lethality_risk: HIGH and certain: perinatal lethal from lung agenesis. No Fgf10-null mouse has ever drawn a breath, so there is no viable limbless adult by this route.
specificity: Poor. FGF10 is the major ligand for FGFR2b across many organs: Fgf10-null mice also lack thyroid, pituitary and salivary glands, with minor defects in teeth, kidney, hair follicles and digestive organs.
difficulty: low to make, impossible to make viable as a constitutive allele. The conditional version is the route worth proposing (see timing-prx1-creer-fgf10).
what_we_would_run: Nothing computational adds value here; this is the ground-truth amelia phenotype the whole page is calibrated against. If the judge's mice were tetra-amelic AND died at birth, this is the likely mechanism class.
open_questions: The two founding papers DISAGREE about whether the limb bud initiates: Min et al. say initiation was abolished; Sekine et al. say bud formation initiated but outgrowth did not occur. We preserve that disagreement rather than reconciling it, and it matters because it decides whether the lesion is in induction or in maintenance.

title: Fgfr2-IIIb (FGFR2b) isoform null - the receptor side of the same axis
mechanism: Fgfr2 is alternatively spliced into IIIb and IIIc isoforms with different ligand specificities and mutually exclusive tissue distributions. FGFR2b is the epithelial receptor that reads mesenchymal FGF10. Removing only IIIb leaves IIIc intact and so removes one arm of the mesenchymal-epithelial dialogue rather than the whole receptor.
intervention: Cre-mediated excision of the IIIb exon, retaining IIIc expression.
predicted_phenotype: Severe limb defects with a distinctive time course: 'development of these structures appears to initiate, but then fails with the tissues undergoing extensive apoptosis'. Viable until birth. Also severe lung and anterior pituitary defects, plus salivary gland, inner ear, tooth, skin and minor skull abnormalities.

evidence.cite: De Moerlooze L et al. 2000, Development 127:483-92, 'An important role for the IIIb isoform of fibroblast growth factor receptor 2 (FGFR2) in mesenchymal-epithelial signalling during mouse organogenesis'
evidence.finding: 'Fibroblast growth factor receptor 2(IIIb) null mice are viable until birth, but have severe defects of the limbs, lung and anterior pituitary gland. The development of these structures appears to initiate, but then fails with the tissues undergoing extensive apoptosis.'

evidence.cite: Ohuchi H et al. 2000, Biochem Biophys Res Commun 277:643-9, 'FGF10 acts as a major ligand for FGF receptor 2 IIIb in mouse multi-organ development'
evidence.finding: Fgf10-null phenotypes closely parallel FGFR2b-deficient phenotypes across many organs (absent thyroid, pituitary, salivary glands), supporting FGF10 as the major FGFR2b ligand in organogenesis.

lethality_risk: High - viable until birth only, with lung and pituitary agenesis.
specificity: Poor; multi-organ, by construction (the whole point of the receptor is that it serves many epithelia).
difficulty: low to make; same viability dead end as Fgf10.
what_we_would_run: Nothing new. This route earns its place by being the mechanistic mirror of Fgf10 and by showing that 'initiates then apoptoses' is a THIRD phenotypic class distinct from both amelia and truncation - a distinction the existing dossier does not draw.
open_questions: Is the limb defect in Fgfr2-IIIb nulls the same as the Fgf10 null, or milder because other FGFR2b ligands partially compensate? The abstracts do not settle it and we did not read the bodies.

title: Ectodermal WNT3 / beta-catenin - the human tetra-amelia gene
mechanism: Wnt3 is expressed ubiquitously in limb ectoderm and signals through beta-catenin to establish the AER; beta-catenin is also required continuously to MAINTAIN the ridge once induced. Wnt/beta-catenin sits upstream of BMP signalling in AER establishment and interacts with BMPR1A in dorsoventral patterning. In humans a homozygous nonsense allele of WNT3 causes complete absence of all four limbs.
intervention: Mouse: Wnt3 loss, or conditional removal of beta-catenin from ventral limb ectoderm (before induction to prevent the AER, after induction to make an existing AER disappear). Human: the natural WNT3 Q83X allele.
predicted_phenotype: Human WNT3 Q83X homozygotes: TETRA-AMELIA - complete absence of all four limbs, with craniofacial and urogenital defects. Mouse: AER fails to be established; removing beta-catenin after induction makes an existing AER disappear, giving a later and milder truncation. Note Wnt3-null mice are reported early-lethal, which is why the human allele is the informative one.

evidence.cite: Niemann S et al. 2004, Am J Hum Genet 74:558-63, 'Homozygous WNT3 mutation causes tetra-amelia in a large consanguineous family'
evidence.finding: Homozygous nonsense mutation Q83X in WNT3 in four affected fetuses with autosomal recessive tetra-amelia plus craniofacial and urogenital defects. 'Our findings contrast with the observation of early lethality in mice homozygous for null alleles of Wnt3.' First WNT-gene mutation associated with a Mendelian disorder.

evidence.cite: Barrow JR et al. 2003, Genes Dev 17:394-409, 'Ectodermal Wnt3/beta-catenin signaling is required for the establishment and maintenance of the apical ectodermal ridge'
evidence.finding: Conditional removal of beta-catenin in ventral ectodermal cells is sufficient to elicit the mutant limb phenotype; removing beta-catenin AFTER ridge induction results in the disappearance of the AER. Wnt/beta-catenin lies upstream of BMP in AER establishment.

evidence.cite: Soshnikova N et al. 2003, Genes Dev 17:1963-8, 'Genetic interaction between Wnt/beta-catenin and BMP receptor signaling during formation of the AER and the dorsal-ventral axis in the limb'
evidence.finding: beta-catenin is a key regulator of AER formation and of limb dorsoventral axis; it acts downstream of BMPR1A in AER induction but upstream or parallel in dorsoventral patterning.

reversibility: The beta-catenin conditional is the reversible-in-principle version and the only published demonstration that an ALREADY FORMED AER can be made to disappear - which is the cell-biological basis for every timing route on this page.
lethality_risk: High for germline Wnt3 (early embryonic lethal in mouse). The ectoderm-restricted beta-catenin conditional avoids that.
specificity: beta-catenin is the least specific molecule in this entire design space - it is the canonical WNT effector in essentially every tissue. Restriction comes entirely from the Cre driver, not from the gene.
difficulty: medium. Floxed beta-catenin and limb-ectoderm Cre drivers are standard.
what_we_would_run: Nothing new computationally. The value of this route on the page is that it names the human condition the judge is most likely to have in mind if their work is human genetics, and that it separates AER ESTABLISHMENT from AER MAINTENANCE as two different targets.
open_questions: The human-versus-mouse viability discordance for WNT3 is flagged by Niemann et al. themselves and is a second instance of the Ushiki lesson: the same gene, two species, different tolerability.

title: RSPO2 / RNF43 / ZNRF3 - the master switch for limb specification
mechanism: RSPO2 potentiates WNT signalling. An allelic series of recessive human RSPO2 mutations causes tetra-amelia syndrome with lung aplasia, with severity correlating with impaired binding to LGR4/5/6 and to the RNF43 and ZNRF3 transmembrane ligases. Unexpectedly, triple knockout of Lgr4/5/6 in mice does NOT reproduce the Rspo2 phenotype; instead RSPO2 acts as a direct antagonistic ligand of RNF43 and ZNRF3, and deleting rnf43 and znrf3 together in Xenopus triggers outgrowth of SUPERNUMERARY limbs.
intervention: Mouse: Rspo2 loss of function, or an allelic series modelled on the human mutations. The reciprocal (deleting Rnf43/Znrf3) is the limb-ADDITION direction and is the cleanest published demonstration that this node is a bidirectional switch.
predicted_phenotype: Human RSPO2 loss of function: tetra-amelia syndrome - 'lung aplasia and a total absence of the four limbs'. The published allelic series means severity is graded, not binary. In mouse, the corresponding Rspo2 limb phenotype is not stated in the abstract we read; we would not assert it.

evidence.cite: Szenker-Ravi E et al. 2018, Nature 557:564-569, 'RSPO2 inhibition of RNF43 and ZNRF3 governs limb development independently of LGR4/5/6'
evidence.finding: 'an allelic series of recessive RSPO2 mutations in humans that cause tetra-amelia syndrome, which is characterized by lung aplasia and a total absence of the four limbs'; severity correlated with binding and WNT-potentiation defects. 'the concurrent deletion of rnf43 and znrf3 in Xenopus embryos was sufficient to trigger the outgrowth of supernumerary limbs. Our results establish that RSPO2 ... serves as a direct antagonistic ligand to RNF43 and ZNRF3, which together constitute a master switch that governs limb specification.'

reversibility: Conceptually the most reversible node in the design space, because it is a ligand-receptor antagonism rather than a transcriptional commitment: the Xenopus result shows the switch can be driven in the gain direction too. Whether that is tractable in mouse is untested.
lethality_risk: High in the full loss-of-function state - lung aplasia accompanies the human amelia, the same coupling as Fgf10. A graded allele from the human series is the way round it, which is what makes the allelic series valuable.
difficulty: medium-high. Point alleles from the human series are straightforward to knock in; interpreting them needs the lung phenotype controlled.
what_we_would_run: If a sequence/protein model is going to be tested on 'does this variant abolish limb development', the RSPO2 allelic series is a better-posed coding benchmark than anything in the ZRS literature, because severity is graded, the biochemistry is measured per allele, and the phenotype is recorded per family.
open_questions: What is the mouse Rspo2 limb phenotype, and does it match the human? We did not retrieve it; stating it would be fabrication.
This gene is absent from the existing dossier and is arguably a stronger candidate than WNT3 for 'the gene for limblessness' in human genetics.

title: Tbx5 - forelimb only, and the cleanest single-pair route
mechanism: TBX5 is expressed exclusively in the prospective forelimb mesenchyme before any bud is visible. It directly activates Fgf10 through a conserved binding site, which is how it initiates the FGF/WNT loop. Critically, the limb FIELD is still patterned correctly in its absence: the territory is specified, the bud is simply never started. Tbx5 is also required later for continued outgrowth.
intervention: Germline Tbx5 null, or Cre-conditional deletion in the forelimb field. Human TBX5 haploinsufficiency gives Holt-Oram syndrome (upper-limb and heart defects), which is a much milder phenotype and should not be quoted as limblessness.
predicted_phenotype: FORELIMB BUDS DO NOT FORM. Hindlimbs are normal. Patterning of the lateral plate mesoderm into the limb field is intact; the FGF and Wnt regulatory loops are never established, including initiation of Fgf10 expression. Early forelimb-versus-hindlimb identity is not disturbed.

evidence.cite: Agarwal P et al. 2003, Development 130:623-33, 'Tbx5 is essential for forelimb bud initiation following patterning of the limb field in the mouse embryo'
evidence.finding: 'mouse embryos lacking Tbx5 do not form forelimb buds, although the patterning of the lateral plate mesoderm into the limb field is intact. Tbx5 is not essential for an early establishment of forelimb versus hindlimb identity. In the absence of Tbx5, the FGF and Wnt regulatory loops required for limb bud outgrowth are not established, including initiation of Fgf10 expression. Tbx5 directly activates the Fgf10 gene via a conserved binding site.'

evidence.cite: Rallis C et al. 2003, Development 130:2741-51, 'Tbx5 is required for forelimb bud formation and continued outgrowth'
evidence.finding: Conditional knockout in the developing forelimb shows Tbx5 is required at early limb bud stages for forelimb bud development; dominant-negative/dominant-active misexpression in chick wing shows a further requirement at later stages for continued outgrowth. Human TBX5 haploinsufficiency causes Holt-Oram syndrome.

reversibility: A conditional allele plus an inducible Cre makes this the best-documented STAGE-SELECTABLE single-pair route, because Rallis et al. show there are two separable requirements (initiation and continued outgrowth).
lethality_risk: Medium. TBX5 is a cardiac transcription factor and the germline null has heart defects; a limb-restricted conditional removes that problem. This is the whole argument for conditional over germline.
specificity: Forelimb only - the single most specific route in the gene scale. Hindlimbs untouched.
difficulty: low-medium. Floxed Tbx5 and limb Cre drivers are standard reagents.
what_we_would_run: Our pattern simulators can model an initiation failure (no FGF10 source) versus a maintenance failure (source decays) and ask whether the two give distinguishable bud-size trajectories. That is a model-internal claim about our own simulator, not a claim about mice, and we would label it as such.
open_questions: A forelimb-only animal still has hindlimbs and so can locomote, thermoregulate and reach food - which is why this route, not tetra-amelia, is the one with a plausible welfare case. Whether a mouse without forelimbs can groom adequately is a question for a veterinary assessment, not for us.

title: Tbx4 (with Pitx1) - hindlimb only, and a very narrow time window
mechanism: Tbx4 is the hindlimb counterpart of Tbx5 and is required for hindlimb bud outgrowth; Pitx1 sits with it in the posterior lateral plate and determines hindlimb morphological identity. The conditional analysis is the interesting part: ablating Tbx4 before hindlimb-field expression blocks outgrowth, ablating it shortly after onset leaves outgrowth and Fgf10 expression unaffected but reduces limb core tissue, and ablating it later produces no defect at all.
intervention: Germline Tbx4 null; or the conditional allele ablated at chosen stages; or Pitx1 null. Pitx1 misexpression in the forelimb transforms forelimb muscle, tendon and bone towards hindlimb morphology, so the gene is a morphology switch in both directions.
predicted_phenotype: Tbx4 null: the hindlimb field IS induced and initial bud patterning appears normal, but buds fail to develop and do not maintain Fgf10; embryos die by E10.5 from failed chorioallantoic fusion, with stunted apoptotic allantoises and no vascular remodelling. Pitx1 null: hindlimb development severely impaired but NOT abolished - ilium and knee cartilage absent, long bones underdeveloped, Tbx4 reduced. Tbx4 loss does not alter hindlimb IDENTITY by morphology or molecular markers.

evidence.cite: Naiche LA & Papaioannou VE 2003, Development 130:2681-93, 'Loss of Tbx4 blocks hindlimb development and affects vascularization and fusion of the allantois'
evidence.finding: Homozygous nulls 'fail to undergo chorioallantoic fusion and die by 10.5 days post coitus'. 'Induction of a hindlimb field occurs normally in Tbx4 mutants and initial patterning of the hindlimb bud appears normal. However, hindlimb buds from Tbx4 mutants fail to develop either in vivo or in vitro and do not maintain Fgf10 expression in the mesenchyme.'

evidence.cite: Naiche LA & Papaioannou VE 2007, Development 134:93-103, 'Tbx4 is not required for hindlimb identity or post-bud hindlimb outgrowth'
evidence.finding: Ablation before hindlimb-field expression confirms a requirement for bud outgrowth; ablation shortly after onset 'alters neither limb outgrowth nor expression of Fgf10' but gives reduced limb core tissue and proximal hypoplasia; later loss 'produces no limb defects, revealing a brief developmental requirement for Tbx4 function'. Loss of Tbx4 has no effect on hindlimb identity.
Pitx1 null: hindlimb severely impaired not abolished; ilium and knee cartilage absent; also loss of proximal mandible-derived bones.

evidence.cite: DeLaurier A, Schweitzer R & Logan M 2006, Dev Biol 299:22-34, 'Pitx1 determines the morphology of muscle, tendon, and bones of the hindlimb'
evidence.finding: Misexpression of Pitx1 in the forelimb transforms and translocates specific muscles, tendons and bones toward hindlimb-like morphology and upregulates Hoxc10 and Tbx4; misexpression of Tbx4 does not. 'Pitx1, but not Tbx4, determines the morphological identity of hindlimb tissues.'

reversibility: The published conditional series is the point: there is a brief window in which Tbx4 matters and outside it the gene is dispensable. That is a real, measured timing knob, not a proposal.
lethality_risk: The germline Tbx4 null is lethal at E10.5 for an allantoic reason entirely unrelated to limbs - a textbook case of a non-limb phenotype masquerading as a limb result. The conditional allele is what makes the route usable at all.
specificity: Hindlimb only, if conditional. The germline allele also hits the allantois; Pitx1 also hits the mandible.
difficulty: medium. Conditional allele and stage-specific Cre both published.
what_we_would_run: Encode the Tbx4 timing result as a test case for our coupling layer: the SAME genetic lesion produces three different phenotypes depending only on when it is applied. Any claim of the form 'gene X -> phenotype Y' that carries no time index should be refused by the layer, and this is the cleanest published example to anchor that rule on.
open_questions: Is there an equivalently narrow window for Tbx5 in the forelimb? Rallis et al. report two requirements but we did not find a stage-resolved series as fine as Naiche's.
